posts.title: How to Read a Peptide Certificate of Analysis (COA)
posts.targetKeyword: how to read a peptide COA
posts.seoDescription: Learn how to read a peptide Certificate of Analysis, match the lot number to your label, and understand the reported test results and specifications.
posts.excerpt: Learn how to read a peptide Certificate of Analysis, match the lot number to your label, and understand the reported test results and specifications.
posts.bodyHtml:
A Certificate of Analysis, or COA, records the results reported for a particular material and lot. If you have a Peptiva certificate open, start at the top of the document. The identifiers there tell you whether the results belong with the vial or inventory record you’re reviewing.

Match the report to the material

Find the material name and lot number on the certificate. Compare both with the label or the lot entry in your lab’s records. Include any letters, leading zeros, and suffixes in the comparison. The same material can appear in several reports, each associated with a different lot.

Then find the date beside the report’s issue or reporting field. Record that date and the report or accession number if one appears. With those details, a colleague can retrieve the same document later, even if the supplier’s page has since added a more recent lot.

Read across each result row

Start with the name of the test. Read across to the reported result, its unit or format, and any specification listed for that test. A specification states the criterion used to interpret the result. If the report lists a method, qualifier, or footnote, read it with the corresponding row. Copy the result with those details when they affect its interpretation.

See the fields on a published COA

On the published GHK-Cu certificate, the material is listed as GHK-CU and the lot is D4129. The report is dated July 23, 2026. It reports purity of 99.28% and lists net peptide content as “Not Requested.” A record based on that certificate could preserve the material, lot, date, and both entries so a reader knows which field contains a value and which carries a status.

When a field is blank, check the footnotes and any continuation pages. If the information is needed for your record, ask about that specific field using the material name, lot, and report ID. To find the certificate that belongs with your own label, start with the Peptiva COA library.

posts.title: What Are Research Peptides? A Laboratory Introduction
posts.seoDescription: Get a plain-English introduction to research peptides, how they differ from proteins, and where researchers can check a material’s lab documentation.
posts.excerpt: Get a plain-English introduction to research peptides, how they differ from proteins, and where researchers can check a material’s lab documentation.
posts.bodyHtml:
Peptides are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Amino acids are the individual building blocks, and a peptide bond connects one building block to the next. The order of the amino acids in the resulting chain is its sequence. Two chains can contain the same building blocks in a different order and be distinct peptides. The IUPAC Gold Book definition of peptides describes the chemical bond behind that distinction.

How peptides relate to proteins

Proteins are also built from chains of amino acids. In everyday scientific usage, peptide often refers to a shorter chain, while protein typically refers to one or more longer chains that fold into a characteristic structure. The vocabulary varies across fields. For a precise identification, use the material name and the description given in the specific publication, catalog, or report.

What research use describes

In “research peptide,” research describes the context the supplier identifies for the material. On Peptiva, that context is laboratory research. A listing might show a material name and a stated amount, while the container or its associated paperwork can supply the lot number. The Peptiva FAQ explains how the company describes research use on its site.

You may see that one material name appears in multiple listings. Check the listed format and amount when reading the catalog. Once a label gives you a lot number, retain the written identifier with your record so you can retrieve the specific document associated with that material.

Where the certificate fits

A Certificate of Analysis, commonly shortened to COA, lists the tests and results reported for the lot named in the document. Depending on the report, the results may include identity, purity, or other fields. Read the document alongside the label so you can tell which records refer to the package you have and which refer to a different lot.

If this is your first time opening a lab report, use our guide to reading a peptide COA to find the identifiers and read the result rows in context.

posts.title: How to Read a Research Peptide Label
posts.targetKeyword: how to read a research peptide label
posts.seoDescription: Read the material name, lot number, and research-use wording on a peptide label, and check which details connect the package to its paperwork.
posts.excerpt: Read the material name, lot number, and research-use wording on a peptide label, and check which details connect the package to its paperwork.
posts.bodyHtml:
A research peptide label gives you the information you need to identify a container in your records. Start with its full material name and the amount or format printed on the package. Then locate the lot number. Reading the three fields together makes it easier to retrieve the corresponding lab report.

Read the material name and stated amount

Copy the complete name, including any form or suffix that appears in print. If the label lists an amount, copy the number and unit together. Record what the number describes as written. For example, a receiving record can have a field called “Label amount” and a separate field for a value that appears under a named measurement in the certificate.

Several catalog entries can share a material name, so keep the stated format or amount with the name when comparing the package against an order record. For a refresher on how these listings describe materials, see our introduction to research peptides.

Copy the lot as printed

Look for “Lot,” “Lot No.,” “Batch,” or a similar field name. Copy the full value, including letters, punctuation, and any leading zeros. If the print is difficult to read, check the outer packaging or associated order paperwork. Record where you found the identifier and ask the supplier to confirm it if the sources differ.

Find the intended use and the matching report

Read any wording about research use and note its location if the receiving record asks for it. Next, find the material in the Peptiva COA library. Open the PDF and compare the lot printed on it against the label. A matching name and lot let you connect the certificate and the container to the same records entry.

For a simple label record, use three lines. Write the material name and labeled amount on the first line, the exact lot number on the second, and the research-use wording as printed on the third. Save the matching certificate link with the entry so the next person can find the source.

posts.title: How to Find the COA for Your Peptide Lot
posts.targetKeyword: find Peptiva COA by lot number
posts.seoDescription: Find a Peptiva Certificate of Analysis by matching your lot number to the published report. See what information to share if you need help finding it.
posts.excerpt: Find a Peptiva Certificate of Analysis by matching your lot number to the published report. See what information to share if you need help finding it.
posts.bodyHtml:
If you have a Peptiva vial in hand, use the label’s material name and lot number to find its Certificate of Analysis. A product page can contain records for more than one lot, so confirm the number inside the PDF before saving it to your records.

Start with the label

Copy the material name exactly as printed and note the amount or form if it helps identify the listing. Write down the full lot number. For codes such as D4129, both the letter and digits are part of the identifier. Keep the original label or a clear image handy while you search.

Open the relevant certificate

Find the material in the Peptiva COA library and open the available report. You can also find GHK-Cu lot reports on its product page. Search the PDF for the copied lot number or read the lot field in the report header. Compare its exact value with your label and record the report ID or accession number when available.

For example, opening the published GHK-Cu certificate for D4129 reveals D4129 in the lot field. For a package with the same material name and lot, file that report alongside the lot entry. A package showing a different lot number needs a document with its corresponding identifier.

Ask for the exact report if needed

If the list has no matching PDF or the label is difficult to read, use the Peptiva contact page. Share the material name, printed lot number, and the report link you checked, if you have one. An order reference can help support locate the record. If you include a photo, make sure the material name and lot are readable.

Once you have the matching PDF, record the link and report date with your receiving entry. Keeping the file or a dated reference helps you retrieve the same lot’s record as the catalog adds reports for later deliveries.

posts.title: Understanding Peptide Identity, Purity, and Content
posts.seoDescription: Understand the difference between peptide identity, purity, and measured content, and learn why they appear as separate entries on a lab report.
posts.excerpt: Understand the difference between peptide identity, purity, and measured content, and learn why they appear as separate entries on a lab report.
posts.bodyHtml:
Identity, purity, and content can each appear on a Certificate of Analysis. They describe different findings, so keep their field names attached to their values when you copy them into a lab record.

What each field answers

FieldQuestion it answersWhat to copy
IdentityWhat material did the reported test identify?The identity value or conclusion as printed.
PurityWhat purity did the reported method indicate?The value and its format, with the method if listed.
ContentWhat amount did the report measure for the named field?The value and unit, or the precise status shown.

An identity entry might use the material name or state that it matches the report’s reference. A purity entry may be a percentage. Its interpretation depends on the test and how the report defines the measurement. Content, when measured, gives an amount for the field specified, such as a value in mass units. Check which quantity the report describes before recording it.

Read the GHK-Cu example

On the published GHK-Cu certificate for lot D4129, the identity entry reads “GHK-CU.” The report lists 99.28% under purity, while the net peptide content entry reads “Not Requested.” In a lot record, preserve that wording under the content field. The amount printed on a package, if you record it, can go in a separately labeled field for the stated amount.

Add context to your notes

If a report includes a specification or note next to a finding, copy it with the relevant row. When the report uses an abbreviation, look for its explanation in the legend or footnotes. If you need a measurement that has no reported value, ask about the named field and provide the lot and report ID.

Use the guide to reading a peptide COA to locate each result alongside its test name, specification, and any notes that explain how to read it.

posts.title: What Does Research Use Only (RUO) Mean?
posts.targetKeyword: research use only meaning on a peptide label
posts.seoDescription: Learn what Peptiva means by Research Use Only, where you’ll see the designation, and which documents to review for laboratory records.
posts.excerpt: Learn what Peptiva means by Research Use Only, where you’ll see the designation, and which documents to review for laboratory records.
posts.bodyHtml:
Research Use Only, often abbreviated RUO, is the wording Peptiva uses to describe materials supplied to qualified researchers for laboratory use. If you are reviewing a label or listing for your lab, the designation tells you the intended setting. The matching documentation supplies the lot and report details your team may need for its records.

Where to find the designation

Look for the written statement on the supplier’s site and the wording on the packaging. If your receiving record has a field for intended use, capture the phrase as it appears and note the source, such as the label or the supplier’s FAQ. This gives a colleague a way to confirm which wording you read.

The Peptiva FAQ is a starting point for questions about the company’s research-use policy. Peptiva’s stated scope is laboratory research for qualified researchers. For definitions of the material and listing fields, see the introduction to research peptides.

What to file with the label

Record the material name and lot number exactly as they appear on the packaging. If your lab needs the supplier’s Certificate of Analysis, open the Peptiva COA library, find the material, and check that the lot printed in the certificate matches the lot on the label. Record the designation and the certificate link in their own fields so the source of each detail is clear.

How to ask about a specific record

If your team needs a document or has a question about Peptiva’s requirements, start with the material name and lot. Specify what you need, such as confirmation of the label wording or a copy of the report associated with the lot. Include the label or page you consulted if that context helps. Use the Peptiva contact page for questions about the material or its documentation.

posts.title: What Lot Numbers, SKUs, and Report IDs Mean
posts.targetKeyword: lot number vs SKU vs report ID
posts.seoDescription: Learn which code identifies a catalog item, which identifies a lot, and which identifies a lab report. See how to record all three accurately.
posts.excerpt: Learn which code identifies a catalog item, which identifies a lot, and which identifies a lab report. See how to record all three accurately.
posts.bodyHtml:
The code on a catalog listing, the code on a vial, and the number on a lab report can all refer to the same material at different levels. Use the SKU to identify the catalog item, the lot number to identify the material’s lot, and the report ID to retrieve a specific document.

What each identifier points to

IdentifierWhat it identifiesWhere to look
Stock keeping unit (SKU)A catalog or inventory item, often a particular size or format.Product listing, inventory record, or order paperwork.
Lot numberA defined lot associated with the material.Container label, packaging, and the lot field in the report.
Report IDThe document or lab record that the issuer can look up.Certificate header, often labeled report number or accession.

A supplier might receive two lots of the same catalog item. The SKU can stay the same across those lots while each container carries its own lot number. A lab may also issue more than one document concerning a lot, so keep each report’s ID and date with its certificate.

See the difference on a published report

On the GHK-Cu certificate, D4129 is the lot number and 2602040016 is the accession number. A reader matching a vial to the report uses D4129. A reader asking the issuing organization about the specific document can provide the accession number alongside the material and lot. See the label-reading guide for tips on copying the lot code from the package.

Give the codes separate fields

In an inventory record, create one field for the SKU, one for the lot, and one for the report ID. Copy each with any letters or leading zeros, and retain the label if it uses a different name for an identifier. When you need the corresponding certificate, use the lot lookup guide to compare the lot printed on the label with the value in the PDF.

posts.title: What Do the Dates on a Lab Report Mean?
posts.targetKeyword: how to read lab report dates
posts.seoDescription: Learn how to read the dates on a lab report, tell receipt and report dates apart where listed, and copy them into your records with the right labels.
posts.excerpt: Learn how to read the dates on a lab report, tell receipt and report dates apart where listed, and copy them into your records with the right labels.
posts.bodyHtml:
Dates on a lab report tell you which events the issuer recorded. One date may describe when the sample arrived, another when a test took place, and another when the issuer released the report. Read the label beside each date before copying it into your records.

Identify the event beside the date

A “Received Date” ordinarily identifies when the issuing lab received the sample. A test date, if listed, identifies when a particular test or a set of tests took place. “Reported Date” or “Issue Date” generally identifies when the issuer released the report. If a document uses an unfamiliar field name, check its notes or ask the issuer what the field means.

Your own receipt date can describe a different event, such as the date your lab received a delivery. Store that value in the receiving record and keep its label distinct from the date on the certificate.

Read the dates on a sample certificate

The published GHK-Cu certificate for lot D4129 shows these two dates.

Printed fieldDate shown
Received DateJuly 21, 2026
Reported DateJuly 23, 2026

In your notes, you could record both entries with their printed names and leave the testing-date field marked “Unspecified on this report” if your template includes one. If a testing date matters to your record, ask about that event using the material, lot, and accession number.

Make the entries easy to sort

A consistent date format such as 2026-07-23 sorts cleanly in a spreadsheet. Pair it with the field name so the meaning travels with the date. If your system has a single general date field, include the date type in the notes and save the certificate link for reference.

For help finding the document’s date and identifiers, use the guide to reading a peptide COA with the PDF open.

posts.title: How to Spot Missing Fields on a Lab Report
posts.targetKeyword: not requested meaning on a COA
posts.seoDescription: See how to document blank fields and “Not Requested” notes on a lab report, and learn what to ask when a measurement matters to your records.
posts.excerpt: See how to document blank fields and “Not Requested” notes on a lab report, and learn what to ask when a measurement matters to your records.
posts.bodyHtml:
A blank result field and a field labeled “Not Requested” give you different amounts of information. Look at the whole row and any notes before recording what the report says. If the field matters to your records, describe the gap precisely so a colleague or supplier can answer it.

Look beyond the result cell

Read the test name, the result column, and any footnote or legend attached to the row. Check the following page if the report continues. A value written with a symbol, such as a less-than sign, belongs in the record with that qualifier and its unit. If you see an abbreviation, use the report’s own definition when one is supplied.

For an empty cell, you could record “No value shown in the result field.” For a status such as “Not Requested,” use those exact words. If a test field is absent from the document, record that you could not locate the field and note the version you checked.

See how an unrequested field appears

On the published GHK-Cu certificate for lot D4129, “Not Requested” appears on the net peptide content line. That is the entry to preserve in your record for that field. The purity field separately reports 99.28%. The guide to identity, purity, and content explains what each of these result fields describes.

Ask a question the supplier can answer

When you need a value for a particular field, include the material name, lot, report ID, and the field’s exact label in your message. You might ask, “Is a separate document available that reports net peptide content for lot D4129?” Include the PDF link if you have it so support can see the same report you reviewed.

File the response with the original notes. If you receive a separate document, identify its date and report number when you update the entry. Use Peptiva’s contact page to ask about a field on a published Peptiva report.

posts.title: How to Check Who Issued a Lab Report
posts.targetKeyword: how to verify a lab report issuer
posts.seoDescription: Check the issuing organization, report ID, and stated scope on a lab report. Learn where to look when you need to confirm the original document.
posts.excerpt: Check the issuing organization, report ID, and stated scope on a lab report. Learn where to look when you need to confirm the original document.
posts.bodyHtml:
To find out who issued a lab report, start with the organization named on the document itself. A supplier may host a certificate on its website while the PDF identifies the laboratory or organization that released it. The issuer’s name, report number, and date give you a way to refer to the exact report.

Check the identifying details in the PDF

Look in the header and on the last page for the issuing organization and any contact details listed with the report. Copy the name as printed. Then find the report, accession, or reference number and its associated date. If the PDF has several pages, check that the page count or document identifiers connect them to the same report.

On the published GHK-Cu certificate for lot D4129, the report names Freedom Diagnostics and lists accession 2602040016. Those details identify the issuing organization named in that copy and the reference attached to it.

Confirm the material and scope

Check the material name and lot number near the header. Then read the listed test names to see what the document covers. If you are logging a specific result, preserve the test label and any qualifier along with the report ID. The guide to reading a peptide COA shows how to connect those details.

Verify the source copy when you need it

Start with the PDF linked in the Peptiva COA library. If a forwarded copy looks incomplete, compare the issuer, date, page count, and report ID with the supplier’s published version. If you need confirmation from the issuer, look for an official verification option or current contact channel for that organization and quote the report number.

A compact review note can record the issuer, report ID and date, material and lot, and the source URL you checked. Add the date of your review so the next person knows which copy was available at the time.

posts.title: How to Request a Missing Certificate of Analysis
posts.targetKeyword: how to request a missing COA
posts.seoDescription: Use a short request template to ask Peptiva for a missing Certificate of Analysis. Gather the material name and exact lot number before reaching out.
posts.excerpt: Use a short request template to ask Peptiva for a missing Certificate of Analysis. Gather the material name and exact lot number before reaching out.
posts.bodyHtml:
If you can see the lot number on the label but cannot find its Certificate of Analysis online, you can ask Peptiva to look up the document. A concise request with the exact material and lot gives support the information it needs to start.

Check for an existing certificate

Find the material in the Peptiva COA library, open the relevant PDF, and compare its lot field with your label. The lot lookup guide walks through the steps. If the report lists a different lot, copy that number separately and save the link. It helps support identify the document you ruled out.

Send a request with the label details

Copy the material name, labeled amount or format if shown, and lot number. Include an order reference if you have one. If the lot is unclear, attach a readable photo of the relevant part of the label and tell support which character is hard to read.

Certificate request template

Subject — Certificate of Analysis request for [material name], lot [lot number]

Hello Peptiva team,

Could you send me the Certificate of Analysis for the material listed below?

Material name and labeled amount or format — ___

Lot number as printed — ___

Order reference, if available — ___

Report link already checked, if applicable — ___

Thank you.

Submit your request through the Peptiva contact page. If your lab needs a particular field in addition to the certificate, include its name so support can address that question in the same reply.

File the response with your lot

When you receive the report, compare the material and lot in the PDF with the label once more. Save the copy and its link with the lot record, then add the report date and ID if present. Keep the response if it explains a discrepancy or supplies context your next reviewer will need.

posts.title: How to Read a Result Against Its Specification
posts.seoDescription: See how a lab report shows a result alongside its stated specification. Learn where to find units, limits, and any interpretation the report provides.
posts.excerpt: See how a lab report shows a result alongside its stated specification. Learn where to find units, limits, and any interpretation the report provides.
posts.bodyHtml:
A test result tells you what the report found. The specification tells you the criterion the report uses to interpret that finding. Read them together with the test name and unit so you can record exactly what the comparison covers.

Find the value and its format

Start at the left side of the row with the test name. Identify the reported result and how it is expressed. Some entries are measurements with a unit. Others show a percentage or a written finding. Keep signs and qualifiers attached to the value, and look at the notes if the result uses an abbreviation.

Compare the result with the stated criterion

A specification can be an interval, a minimum or maximum, or a description of what must match. Check the unit and any symbols alongside the stated criterion. Here is an illustrative measurement for a sample pin.

TestReported resultStated specification
Pin length10.2 mm10.0–10.5 mm

The reported length is within the interval shown in this example. Any status issued by a testing organization belongs in the record as printed. When only the values appear, you can preserve the row as written and identify any separate interpretation your lab adds.

Record any notes and qualifiers

If the issuer prints an interpretation, such as “Conforms,” copy it alongside the result and specification. If the criterion is absent, mark its field “Unspecified on this report” and save the result with the document. If you need a criterion for your internal review, ask which document contains it.

On a peptide certificate, check that the criterion belongs to the same test as the value. The guide to identity, purity, and content explains the scope of those three common fields. Open the full guide to reading a peptide COA for the earlier step of matching the report to the correct lot.

posts.title: A Lab Receiving Checklist for Research Materials
posts.targetKeyword: lab receiving checklist for research materials
posts.seoDescription: Use this lab receiving checklist to check package condition, confirm the material and lot, file the matching COA, and document any discrepancies.
posts.excerpt: Use this lab receiving checklist to check package condition, confirm the material and lot, file the matching COA, and document any discrepancies.
posts.bodyHtml:
A receiving record connects a delivery to the supplier’s documents. Make the entry while the label and order information are available. That gives your team a dated record of what arrived and a place to track any question about the package or paperwork.

Inspect and identify the delivery

Check the outer packaging and record its condition. When the label is available, compare the material name and stated format or amount with the order record. Copy the full lot number from the package and note the date your team received it. If the delivery contains multiple lots, record each lot separately so its certificate can be retrieved later.

Receiving checklist

  • Record the delivery date, supplier, and order reference.

  • Note the packaging condition and retain a photo if it helps document an issue.

  • Compare the labeled material and format with the order. Copy the lot exactly as printed.

  • Open the certificate and check its material name and lot. File the matching link or copy with the receiving record.

  • Record any open issue, who will follow up, and the next action.

The Peptiva lot lookup guide explains how to find the matching certificate and confirm the lot inside the PDF. The Peptiva FAQ provides general information about research use and orders.

Record the discrepancy and its outcome

Describe what you observed using the actual label and document fields. For example, write “Lot shown on label: A0047. Lot shown in the linked PDF: A0049.” Those two entries give a colleague specific values to compare and help support find the right certificate.

Use the Peptiva contact page for questions about a delivery. Include the material name, lot, order reference, and a short description of the issue. Keep any follow-up in the same record and add the date when you receive confirmation or file the corrected documentation.

posts.title: How to Document a Lot Number Mismatch
posts.seoDescription: Record a lot number mismatch between a label and its certificate. See which details to note, what to share with support, and how to log the response.
posts.excerpt: Record a lot number mismatch between a label and its certificate. See which details to note, what to share with support, and how to log the response.
posts.bodyHtml:
Sometimes the material name on a certificate matches the package while the lot number differs. Preserve both numbers in your records. The difference could reflect a link to another lot or a label that needs clarification. Capturing what you saw lets support trace the documents without reconstructing your search.

Compare the two sources

Read the lot field on the label and the one inside the PDF. Copy each exactly, including prefixes, zeros, and suffixes. If you suspect a character was transcribed incorrectly, check the original label or a clear photo. Add the material name, report ID, report date, and link to the file you opened.

Discrepancy note template

Date observed — ___

Material name and order reference — ___

Lot printed on the package — ___

Lot shown in the certificate — ___

Certificate link, report ID, and report date — ___

Issue observed and supporting file or photo — ___

Follow-up owner, status, and resolution date — ___

If the issue was first noticed during delivery, connect the note to the record created using the lab receiving checklist. One entry can capture what arrived, while the discrepancy note tracks the specific question about the paperwork.

Ask for confirmation and log the answer

Send the two lot values, material name, and report details through the Peptiva contact page. Ask for the certificate tied to the printed lot or for confirmation of the correct identifier if the label is unclear.

When support responds, add the date, what they confirmed, and the link to any replacement PDF. Check the new document using the lot lookup guide and record the matching report under the appropriate lot. Keep the original observation with the resolution so your team can see how the record changed.

posts.title: How to Keep Lot Records for Research Materials
posts.seoDescription: Set up a lot tracking record for research materials. See which fields to include, where to file certificates, and how to record changes between lots.
posts.excerpt: Set up a lot tracking record for research materials. See which fields to include, where to file certificates, and how to record changes between lots.
posts.bodyHtml:
A lot record answers two everyday questions. Which lot did your lab receive, and where is its documentation? A spreadsheet or inventory system can handle both if each entry connects the material and lot to a certificate someone else can open.

Decide what belongs in each entry

Start with the supplier, full material name, and lot as printed. Include the receipt date and an order reference if it helps trace the delivery. Add the report ID and date when the certificate provides them. The documentation status can show whether the report is filed or whether a named person is following up.

Sample lot tracking row

This illustrative row uses example values. The certificate field can point to your team’s stored copy or lot-specific record.

MaterialLotReceipt dateCertificate linkDocument status
Reference material AA00472026-10-06Link to filed PDFMatched to label

Record the lot field as text if you use a spreadsheet. That keeps leading zeros and mixed letters and numbers intact when the system sorts the column.

Give the certificate a recognizable file name

Use a pattern a teammate can recognize, such as material_lot_report-date.pdf. Keep the issuer’s report ID in the inventory entry or file name where it helps distinguish multiple documents for the same lot. Open the link from the record to confirm that it reaches the right PDF. The Peptiva COA library is a useful starting point for finding the supplier’s published copies.

Keep the earlier lot history

Create a new lot entry when a delivery arrives with a new lot code. Keep the older entry and its document links so earlier records can still be traced to the right material. For another delivery of the same lot, follow your lab’s record structure for logging a second receipt against that lot.

Use the lab receiving checklist to gather these details when the material arrives.
